title: Toto Wolff says claims Mercedes’ F1 engine is illegal are ‘utter bulls—‘
content:
SAKHIR, Bahrain — Toto Wolff called suggestions that Mercedes’ Formula 1 engine could be illegal “total bulls—” amid the ongoing compression ratios row that he said was a “storm in a teacup.”

It emerged over the winter that Mercedes may have found a way to produce more horsepower from its engine by exceeding F1’s engine compression ratio limit, which relates to the amount of fuel squeezed into the engine before it is burned.

Mercedes sought clarity from F1’s rule maker, the FIA, over the regulations whereby the compression ratios are only measured when the engine is cold, but not when it was active and hot. So long as Mercedes complied with the rules at the time it was measured, then the engine was legal.

The four rival manufacturers — Ferrari, Red Bull/Ford, Honda and Audi — pushed for the FIA to make changes to F1 rulebook ahead of the new season, leading to a statement on Wednesday that confirmed a vote will take place on a possible rule change midway through the season.

The manufacturers, the FIA and F1 will vote in the coming days on to introduce an additional test from Aug. 1 where the compression ratios would also be tested when the engine is at an operating temperature of 130ºC.

Speaking in Thursday’s news conference at the Bahrain International Circuit, Mercedes chief Wolff said he would be comfortable if the vote went either way, and that it “looks like a storm in a teacup” as it does not offer a big advantage to the manufacturer and its customer teams.

“If you have four other PUs (power units, a type of engine) that are putting immense pressure on the FIA at a certain stage, what choice do we have than not to play?” Wolff said.

“We were pretty comfortable in even having a protest going on on Friday in Melbourne. But is this what we want?”

Wolff was then asked about suggestions that Mercedes had not been running the new, fully sustainable fuels that have been introduced to F1 this year during testing.

“This is another of the stories,” Wolff said. “We were told compression ratio is something that we were illegal, which is total bulls—, utter bulls—. And now the next story comes out that our fuel is illegal.

“I don’t know where that comes from, and it starts spinning again.”

Wolff referred to the fuel question marks as being “another nonsense,” adding that it was “a complicated topic and the process and all of this, but there’s just not… I can’t even comment.”

There has been no mandate from the FIA that teams must use the new fuels through preseason, and a Mercedes spokesperson declined to reveal what type of fuel the team had been using at testing beyond it being supplied by Petronas.

The e-vote proposed by F1’s Power Unit Advisory Committee will take place in the coming days over the new hot test introduction. Should it get support from five out of seven parties, then it will become part of the regulations from Aug. 1.

But Wolff did not think there would be any advantage to be gained for the rival manufacturers, suggesting they may have been looking to remove the cold tests.

“I think the way it’s been done now, and it needs to be compliant to the regulations, when it’s cold and when it’s hot, it doesn’t give anybody any advantage,” Wolff said.

“Because the attempt was from the other guys to only have it measured hot so they could actually have it cold outside of the regulations.

“So now it’s a fair game for everyone.”
